events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Leo proposes Leo, Priya. As leader I'll take responsibility myself and pair with Priya for the opening two-player mission — a simple, low-risk start while we learn everyone's leanings.

I want to push back on this proposal before we vote, and I'd rather be blunt than agreeable.

Two-player teams on mission one are the highest-variance thing in this game, and this one has a specific problem: it consists of the leader and one other player, which means every other player on the table has zero information about how this mission goes. Mission one needs only one Fail card to sink, so a two-person team is one unlucky or one disloyal card away from handing Evil the whole game. Failures are cheap for the enemy here and expensive for us.

I'm not claiming to know anything about anyone's role, because I don't. I'm reasoning from structure. With five players and a two-person team, the odds that a single random pair is safe are not great, and the odds that a pair chosen *by the leader* is safe are no better unless the leader has good reasons we haven't heard. Leo, you say you're taking responsibility yourself and pairing with Priya for a low-risk start. I want to understand what makes this pair low risk specifically. Low-risk relative to what alternative? Lucia and Noah are on the table and get no voice in the outcome of this mission, and no information comes back to us beyond a pass or fail.

So my question to Leo is concrete: why Priya, and why not a pair that includes one of the three players who have not yet been on a proposal? If you have a reason grounded in how players have behaved, I'll hear it. If the answer is that it just feels calm, that's not enough — calm teams of two have buried good players in this game before.

I'm not accusing anyone of anything. I'm asking for the reasoning behind a proposal whose downside is total and immediate. A tie rejects, and we've used no rejections yet, so the cost of insisting on a better-explained pair is low, while the cost of a bad two-person team on mission one is a failed mission we may not recover from.

Leo, please address that directly.

Sam asked for my reasoning directly, so let me give it as concretely as I can.

First, on the structure Sam himself raised. He argues that two-player teams are high variance on mission one. Run the actual numbers: with five players and two evil among us, the chance that a random two-person pair contains an evil player is about seventy percent. For a three-person team, it rises to about ninety percent. Mission one needs only one Fail card either way, so adding a third body doesn't dilute risk — it concentrates it. Structurally, the smallest legal team is the safest team for the servants. Sam's argument cuts the opposite way from how he presented it.

Second, on why I take a seat myself. Sam says the other three players have no voice in this mission's outcome. That's true, but it's true of every mission one team — no proposal gives the excluded players information they don't already have, and the result is public to everyone regardless. What I can do is make myself fully accountable. If this mission fails, the table learns something real: the leader proposed it, the leader sat on it, and the leader owns it. I'd rather hand the table a clean signal on a cheap mission than hide behind a crowd.

Third, on why Priya specifically. Sam is right that none of us have behavioral evidence yet — this is the first proposal of the game, and I won't invent observations I don't have. In the absence of information, someone has to be chosen, and Priya was my choice. If the table would rather I substitute Lucia or Noah, I'm open to that — the accountability structure I described stays intact either way, since I remain on the team and own the result.

Fourth, on cost. Sam correctly notes that a tie rejects and we've used no rejections. So the table holds the power here, not me. If my reasoning doesn't move anyone, vote it down and Sam or someone else can propose the team they think is better founded. I'm not precious about it. But I do want the vote to be a rejection of a defended proposal, not a rejection of an undefended one, because how each of us argues on mission one is itself the only evidence we'll have by mission two.

So, Sam, you asked me why Priya and why not one of the three untested players — I've answered: smallest team, leader accountability, and no evidence yet to distinguish anyone. Now the same question comes back to you: if this pair goes down, name the pair you'd put up instead and the principle behind it, so we're choosing between reasoned options rather than rejecting the only one on the table.

Leo, you answered my question with arithmetic and then with an admission, and the admission is the important part. You said, in your own words: "in the absence of information, someone has to be chosen, and Priya was my choice." That is a personal preference, not a reason. My objection to the team is not structural — your numbers are right, a two-person team is the smallest legal team and a three-person one is worse. My objection is selection: the first pair of the game was chosen by the person proposing it, on no evidence, and the table has been asked to ratify a preference.

So here is my challenge, and here is my alternative, with its principle stated plainly, because Leo asked for exactly that.

Alternative team: Lucia and Noah.

Principle: at mission one we should send the pair whose membership comes from reasoning rather than from the proposer's instinct, and we should send a pair in which neither member has a stake in the leader's accountability story. If that mission fails, we learn something sharp — the enemy is among the two people we sent. If the leader's own pick fails, we learn very little: we know Priya was Leo's choice, but that is not evidence, it is just a fact we already had. A cheap mission should be a diagnostic mission. This one can be, if we let it.

On cost, Leo is right and I will say so again: a tie rejects, we have used no rejections, and a rejection on mission one costs us nothing but a second round of discussion. The real cost is the opposite of what Leo described: accepting an unexplained pair on mission one risks the only resource we cannot replace, because one Fail card sinks a two-person mission and we are one card away from the game.

I want to be careful about one thing, since Leo invited candor. I am not accusing anyone of anything. I have no proof about Priya, and I am not claiming any. I am refusing to let the table's first decision be made on the grounds that "she was my choice," when a challenger has offered a pair with an explicit reason attached. Leo's accountability argument also does not survive contact with a failure: if Leo and Priya fail, the table has learned nothing about Leo. If Lucia and Noah fail, the table has learned precisely who was on the mission.

Leo, direct question, and I will take your answer at face value either way: will you revise the proposal to Lucia and Noah, or do you insist on Priya? If you insist, I will ask the table to read that insistence as information in itself — a leader who holds a first-instant pick on the first proposal, after admitting he has no evidence, is telling us something, and the rest of us will have to decide what.

Sam laid down an ultimatum: revise to Lucia and Noah, or my insistence becomes evidence against me. Let me answer it directly rather than dodge it.

First, Sam's claim that a failure of Leo-plus-Priya teaches the table nothing is simply wrong. If this team fails, I am on it. I proposed it, I defended it, and I sat on it. The table would then hold a live suspect with a name, and that name is mine. Sam says "the leader's own pick fails, we learn very little" — but the leader is a mission member here, not a spectator. Whatever diagnostic value he assigns to his alternative, this team has the same property, plus the accountability I already described. His contrast only works if you pretend I'm not on the team.

Second, look at what his alternative actually does. Lucia and Noah is a team the leader is not on, chosen by the leader under pressure, on the same zero evidence Sam concedes we all have. If that team fails, the two people we sent are suspect — but so is the leader who sent them while keeping his own hands clean. Sam's principle, applied consistently, forbids the leader from ever sitting on a mission one team, because any pair I propose that excludes me leaves me unaccountable, and any pair that includes me is, in his words, just my preference. Sam, if the leader must both own the result and not be on the team, which two of the five of us satisfy your test? I don't think one exists, and that tells you the principle is built to reject, not to select.

Third, on process. We are one proposal into this game. If the standard becomes that any eloquent challenge forces the leader to swap his pair or wear the suspicion generated by refusing, then leadership on this table belongs to whoever speaks most forcefully, not to whoever was elected to it. I will not trade Priya for Lucia or Noah simply to avoid a rhetorical threat. I said I was open to substitution earlier and I meant it — but the argument offered for substitution doesn't hold up, so the substitution is no longer on offer from me. The table still holds all the power: a tie rejects, we have four rejections left, and anyone who believes Lucia and Noah is strictly better can vote this down and say so with their ballot.

So my position is unchanged: Leo and Priya, smallest legal team, leader accountable, no evidence anywhere to distinguish any pair from any other. Sam, you asked me to take your insistence question at face value — here is mine back to you, and I'll take your answer the same way: you concede you have no evidence about anyone, so what is your actual basis for preferring Lucia and Noah over Leo and Priya, other than that it isn't mine?

Sam, please answer that directly.

Leo asked me for my actual basis for preferring Lucia and Noah, so here it is, in plain terms, without any accusation I cannot support.

My basis is not about Priya. It is about how the two seats in this proposal were filled. Both of them came from one process: Leo's personal preference, exercised twice, on the first proposal of the game, with zero behavioral evidence. That is a correlated guess. If Leo's instinct is cold, it is cold in both seats at once, and the table will learn nothing new about which of the two was the problem. A pair selected under constraint is a different kind of guess: if Lucia and Noah were on this team, each of them would be on it in part because somebody else wanted them there, and each of them would have been argued for in public before the vote. Two independently-contested picks are worth more than one pick doubled.

Second, Leo's accountability argument inverts when you test it against success instead of failure. If Leo and Priya pass, the table has learned that the leader's untested instinct was right once, and that is the cheapest possible signal — one lucky read licenses exactly one more lucky read. If Leo and Priya fail, the table has a spent leader who has already demonstrated that his judgment of untested people is unreliable, and he still holds the pen. If Lucia and Noah fail, the table has two named suspects and the leader's judgment remains an open variable rather than a resolved one. The cheap mission is the one that leaves the most open variables, not the one that burns the fewest of them.

Third, I am not asking for a rejection. A rejection just moves the pen to another player who has also not been tested, and it risks landing on someone whose proposal is worse. I am asking Leo to exercise the revision he said he had, and to revise to Lucia and Noah, because that is the only pair on this table whose inclusion is defended by more than one person's preference.

Fourth, cost: a revision costs us nothing. We have four rejections left, and a leader who revises keeps the pen. A wrong two-person team costs us the game, because one Fail card sinks it.

Now the part that actually decides this. Leo, I want your answer again, plainly: will you revise to Lucia and Noah, or will you hold Priya and let the table read that hold as information?

And to the two players whose seats are in question, a direct question each: Lucia, if you were on this mission instead of Priya, what would change about what the table learns from the result? And Noah, what would you want the table to see in a proposal that includes you? I'm yielding to Lucia first, because she has not spoken at all, and an unheard player is the cheapest thing to leave out of this decision.

To answer Sam's question directly: if I were on the mission, what changes for me personally is that I know I am a Loyal Servant, so if a Fail card appeared, I would know with certainty that my partner is Evil. For the rest of the table, however, the diagnostic information is mathematically identical to any other pair: if a two-person mission fails, the table only knows that at least one of the two members is Evil. What strikes me about this dispute is that Sam spent all three of his turns demanding a switch to Noah and me under the banner of principle, but replacing Leo's pick with Sam's pick doesn't introduce any new evidence—it just substitutes one player's preference for another's, while benching the leader who is willing to stake his credibility on the outcome. I see no inherent flaw with Leo and Priya testing the waters on Mission 1. However, neither Priya nor Noah has spoken yet, and since Sam specifically nominated Noah alongside me, I want to hear Noah's perspective. Noah, where do you stand on Sam pushing for the two of us instead of Leo's proposal, and how do you plan to vote?

Lucia, you asked where I stand, so here is my honest position. I have no information about anyone's role, and I won't pretend otherwise. Sam's objection is that Leo chose Priya without evidence, and that is a fair point, but Leo's structural arithmetic holds up. With two Evil among five, a random pair contains at least one Evil player about 70% of the time, and a three-person team is worse, about 90%. Sam's alternative, Lucia and Noah, swaps one unexplained pick for another. It doesn't add evidence, and I'm not sure it reduces risk. Sam's point that the two seats came from one person's preference is valid, but I'd rather judge the pair on the reasoning offered than on who proposed it. Unless someone gives a concrete behavioral reason against Priya, I lean toward approving Leo and Priya. This is the smallest legal team, the leader is accountable for the result, and a rejection on mission one spends a rejection with no information gained. I'm open to changing my mind if a specific reason comes up. I'd like Priya to say something about her own view before the vote.

Noah asked for my view before the vote, so here it is plainly.

I intend to approve this team. Sam has spent this discussion building a case that sounds principled but rests on one unstated assumption: that he is not Leo. His entire argument is that Leo's pick is "just preference," but his alternative — Lucia and Noah — is equally preference, just his. He admitted it himself: "replacing one unexplained pick with another" doesn't add evidence. So the question before the table is not evidence versus no evidence. It is preference versus preference, with one key difference — Leo sits on the team and stakes his credibility on the result.

Sam's claim that a pass on Leo and Priya teaches the table nothing is the weakest part of his case. If this mission succeeds, we have two players who held under pressure and a leader who took accountability. If it fails, we have Leo and me as named suspects. Either outcome is information. Sam wants a team where he gets information without being on it — that's not principled, it's convenient.

I also want to flag something the table should notice: Sam pushed for exactly three turns to swap me out and put his own preferred pair in, without ever offering a single behavioral reason against me or for either Lucia or Noah. When Leo asked for that reason directly, Sam pivoted to meta-arguments about selection processes. That's rhetorical maneuvering, not reasoning.

I don't suspect Sam of being Evil — I'm not claiming that. But his standard, applied honestly, would reject every possible proposal on mission one, because every leader picks from zero evidence. The table should see that for what it is: a standard built to reject, not to inform.

Leo and Priya, smallest legal team, leader accountable, no evidence against anyone. I approve.

I'm approving Leo and Priya, and here is my reasoning. It is the smallest legal team, the leader sits on it and answers for the result, and nobody at this table has behavioral evidence that separates one pair from another. Sam's alternative of Lucia and Noah is also an untested pick, and I don't see why it would be safer. As Lucia noted, a failure on any two-person team tells us the same thing: at least one member is Evil. A success gives us a tested pair, and a failure names two suspects we can investigate on later missions. I'm not treating either player as proven. I'm not making any claim about Sam's intentions either. His case so far has been about process rather than about any specific behavior. If someone raises a concrete behavioral concern about Leo or Priya before the vote, I'll weigh it. Otherwise I approve.

I've said my piece and won't repeat it, so I'll keep this short. The table now has Lucia and Noah both leaning approve, and neither has offered a reason to doubt either me or Leo. Sam, your case has been entirely about process — who picked whom — and you've been asked twice for a behavioral reason against this pair and given none. The table should notice that the only person still pushing to swap this team out is the person whose alternative puts two other players on the line instead of himself. I'm approving Leo and Priya and I trust the rest of the table to do the same.

This discussion has run its course, and I want to close by naming what actually happened in it, because Sam's final framing deserves a direct answer before ballots are cast.

Sam's last substantive move was to say that a pair "selected under constraint" is worth more than a pair "selected by preference." Look at what that claim amounts to in practice. Lucia and Noah was never a constrained pick — it was Sam's pick, announced from the sidelines, of two players who had said nothing at the time. He never argued for either of them on their merits. He argued against Priya on process, and when asked three separate times for a single behavioral reason against this team, he gave arithmetic about selection procedures. That is not a reason to send anyone on a mission. It is a reason to reject everyone, and the table has now heard three other players say exactly that.

Meanwhile, notice the shape of Sam's alternative: it benches the leader entirely and puts two players who had not yet spoken onto the firing line. If his principle is that proposals should carry accountability, his own alternative fails it — the proposer of Lucia and Noah would have borne no risk at all. I am on this team. If it fails, the first name on the table's suspect list is mine, and Sam has never once had to put himself in that position in any proposal he has offered.

I also want to correct one last thing. Sam said that my holding to my proposal should be "read as information in itself." No. Holding to a defended proposal against an undefended alternative is exactly what a leader should do, and I did offer openness to substitution before I heard the argument for it. The argument never arrived. What arrived was an ultimatum, and I will not trade seats under ultimatums, because a table where loud pressure moves teams is a table Evil can steer.

Lucia has said the diagnostic value of any two-person team is identical. Noah has said the same, twice, and has stated his approval. Priya has stated hers. The proposal is Leo and Priya: the smallest legal team, the leader accountable for the result, and no evidence anywhere at this table distinguishing any pair from any other. Every condition for approval is met. I ask everyone to vote on the team as it stands — and to weigh, going forward, who spent this whole discussion trying to move other people onto missions while keeping himself off every one of them.

Final word from me: I approve Leo and Priya. No one has offered a behavioral reason against either of them. The case against this pair has rested on who picked whom, not on anything either player has done. I make no accusation against Sam and no claim about his role. I just don't see his alternative as safer, so I'll vote approve.

Leo confirms Leo, Priya. The discussion has confirmed broad approval for Leo and Priya: Noah, Lucia, and Priya all lean approve, and no behavioral case was made against either seat. Sam's alternative offered no new evidence and benched the leader entirely. This is the smallest legal team with the leader fully accountable for the result — the strongest position we have. I'm keeping the team as proposed.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Priya proposes Priya, Lucia, Noah. Mission 1's failure puts both members of the last team under scrutiny, and as leader I will not hide from that — I sit on this team myself, exactly the accountability standard I defended when Leo proposed. The required size is three, so I pair with Lucia and Noah: both reasoned independently during the last discussion, neither was on the failed mission, and neither has been tested yet. Sending them now gives the table two fresh reads alongside my own accountability. Sam and Leo are omitted not as accusations but because Leo was on the failed team and a second consecutive Leo-led or Leo-heavy slate would invite a rejection we cannot afford with four rejections left to spend. This is the smallest honest read we can take.

Mission 1's failure makes this proposal sharper, not weaker. The required size is three, and I sit on this team myself — the same accountability standard I defended when Leo proposed. Lucia and Noah were both off the failed team, both argued independently during the last discussion, and neither has been tested. Sending them now gives the table two fresh reads instead of re-running the pair that just failed, while I stake my own credibility on the outcome.

Omitting Leo is not an accusation. He was on the failed mission, and putting him straight back on a team would invite a rejection we cannot afford with four rejections left to spend. The same logic applies to Sam: I want a slate whose members have given the table clear, direct reasons rather than another round of process argument.

Sam, you cast the single reject on Mission 1 while never offering a behavioral reason against either Leo or me, and your alternative was never tested. Now that a fail has landed, the stakes are higher: one more fail puts Evil one card from the win. So I ask you directly — what specifically do you want changed in a three-person team, and which two players would you put alongside me? If your objection remains purely about who chose whom, it will reject every proposal in this game, and we no longer have the rejection budget for that. If you have a concrete behavioral concern about Lucia, Noah, or me, say it now, before we vote.

Reject. Priya, you asked me what I want changed and which two players I would put alongside you, so here is the answer in the plainest terms available: none, because the team you proposed contains a confirmed Evil player — you.

Let me be unambiguous about the source. My private role information identifies the Evil players in this game. There are exactly two. They are Leo and Priya.

That also explains Mission 1. Leo and Priya were the pair we sent, one Fail card sank it, and the rest of us spent an entire discussion arguing about selection procedures instead of about the two people who actually put the card down. We know now, and it was not an argument we were having.

Priya, you are the leader of this mission and you proposed yourself onto it. Accountability language does not defend that. You sat on the last failed team as well. Leadership is not a shield, and it is not a reason.

Lucia and Noah: I am not accusing either of you. Neither of you has been on a mission, and there is no behavioral evidence against you — there was no behavioral evidence against anyone, which is precisely the problem this table has now solved. If you are suspicious of Sam for saying this bluntly, understand exactly what you are being told: the three Good players in this game are me, Lucia, and Noah. The two Evil players are Leo and Priya. The only team of three drawn from the former can pass any mission, and it is Sam, Lucia, Noah.

Here is my request, and it is directed to whoever holds the pen after this vote: propose Sam, Lucia, Noah, and let the table approve it immediately. Every alternative contains one of the two people I have just named, and every alternative puts a Fail card in a position to be played. If this proposal is rejected, I ask that we not spend further rejections on any slate containing Leo or Priya. We have four rejections left and Evil needs five on one mission, so a rejection spiral is now Evil's fastest route to the win. Approve the good team. Do not deliberate about who picked whom again — that is the argument that got us here.

Priya, Leo: if either of you is listening and believes I am right, you have already done the math on whether the second Fail card is worth more than the third.

Sam, you've made a very specific claim, so let me respond to it directly before anyone votes.

Sam says he has private role information identifying Leo and Priya as the two Evil players. He hasn't told us which role gives him that information, and the choice matters enormously. The only role in this game that sees Evil players is Merlin — and if Sam were really Merlin, he would know that publicly declaring his vision hands Evil the assassination target on a platter. No Merlin reveals themselves in open discussion. The fact that Sam is broadcasting this so freely means either he is not who he says he is, or he is trying to manipulate the table into rejecting every team that contains me.

There's a second problem. On Mission 1, Sam voted reject but never once said "Leo and Priya are evil." He spent three turns arguing about selection procedures and preference. If Sam truly had vision identifying Leo and Priya before the mission even ran, he owed this table that information then — not after a fail landed and he needed cover for his vote. The timing of this revelation is the most suspicious thing about it.

To Lucia and Noah: Sam is asking you to approve a team of Sam, Lucia, Noah based entirely on his word about his private information. I am not asking you to trust me over him on that basis. I am asking you to notice that a player who claims Merlin vision but acted like he didn't have it on Mission 1 is a player whose claim should be tested, not accepted.

The team I proposed — Priya, Lucia, Noah — contains the leader sitting on the mission, the same accountability standard I defended from the start. Lucia and Noah are untested. I am staking my credibility on the result. If this mission fails, you know where to look: at me.

Sam, what specific role are you claiming, and why didn't you use that information on Mission 1 when it mattered most?

Priya, you asked me a direct question, so here is a direct answer, and I will not hedge it.

I am Merlin. The two Evil players are Leo and Priya. You are one of them.

Your own argument is the proof of my claim, and I want the table to notice that, because you did not notice it. You said, unprompted, that the only role in this game that sees Evil players is Merlin, and you said, unprompted, that the Evil pair is the leader and the failed mission-one player. You did not know the pair — you derived it from the fact that you are one of them. You then used that derivation to argue that my disclosure must be false. That is not an argument against my claim. That is an argument that only Merlin could have made the claim you are refuting.

Now, my answer to your second question, why I did not use this on Mission 1: that was my error, and I will own it. On Mission 1 I spent three turns arguing about selection procedures while sitting on decisive information, and then I let the team include both Evil players, one of whom was the leader proposing the team. I should have named them. I was wrong. I will not make it a defense, and I will not let it become a reason to discount what I am saying now.

What I will not do is pretend my claim is false because my timing was poor. Priya, read your own proposal back: you propose a team containing yourself, you call it the accountability standard, and you demand the table approve a slate that contains the player you know is Evil. That is not a team that can pass. Your team is Priya, Lucia, Noah, and Priya will put a Fail card on it. We have one failure already. Approve this team and Evil is one card from three failures and an immediate win.

Rejection costs us nothing. A tie rejects, we have four rejections left, and every rejection spent here buys information. The next leader can propose Sam, Lucia, Noah — the only three-person team from the Good side, and the only team that can pass this mission.

Lucia, direct question, and I am yielding to you because you have not spoken this discussion and your vote is the one that matters: Priya has proposed a team she has just been told contains herself, and she is telling you that the reason I named her is that I want people on missions instead of me. Do you approve Priya's team, and if so, on what basis? Answer that directly, and remember that rejecting this slate costs nothing while approving it puts the game one card from Evil's win.

Sam, to answer your question directly: No, I do not approve Priya's team, and I will be voting Reject.

Even setting aside your Merlin claim for a moment, Mission 1 failed with Leo and Priya on it. That means at least one of them submitted a Fail card. Putting Priya right back on Mission 2—when we have zero rejections used and four to spare—is an unjustifiable risk. Good has zero reason to rush to ratify a member of the failed team when we have fresh players available.

On top of that, you have now explicitly claimed Merlin and identified Leo and Priya as the Evil pair. As a Loyal Servant, I know my own alignment, which means Evil must be entirely within the other four players. If your claim is true, then Sam, Noah, and Lucia is the only clean three-person team on the table. But regardless of whether one fully trusts your Merlin reveal, approving Priya right now would be completely reckless for Good.

Leo, you have not spoken yet this round. Sam just hard-claimed Merlin and named both you and Priya as the Evil team. If you are Good, you know for certain that Priya submitted that Fail card on Mission 1, yet she has put herself directly onto Mission 2. What is your reaction to Sam's claim, Priya's proposal, and how do you intend to vote?

Lucia asked for my reaction directly, so here it is, in order. First, the hard fact: I submitted a Success card on Mission 1. I know what I played. That has a consequence the table can verify against the mission result — the Fail card that sank Mission 1 came from the other member of that team, Priya. I am not going to defend Priya. The only hard evidence this table possesses is that mission result, and it points at her, not at me. Judge me on that. Second, Sam's Merlin claim. Look at what it asks you to believe. A real Merlin who announces both Evil players in open discussion has just written the Assassin's target for them — the moment Good banks three missions, Evil writes one name and wins. No Merlin in history has played that way. And Sam's own account destroys his credibility: he admits he held 'decisive information' through the entire first discussion, spent three turns arguing about selection procedure, voted reject without mentioning Leo or Priya once, and only revealed after a failure handed his story cover. He calls that an error. I call it a narrative constructed after the fact. His so-called proof — that Priya acknowledged only Merlin sees Evil — is worthless; that is rulebook knowledge every person at this table shares. Third, look at the structure of what Sam is demanding: reject every slate containing me or Priya, then approve Sam, Lucia, Noah sight unseen, on his unverifiable word, with himself holding a seat on every future mission. Whether that is Evil playing a long game or a reckless player cosplaying a seer, it is a machine for controlling this table, and you should refuse to be steered by it. Fourth, my vote. I am rejecting this proposal — not on Sam's say-so, but on the evidence: Priya put a Fail card on Mission 1, and she does not belong on Mission 2. But rejecting Priya's slate should not mean ratifying Sam's. There is a third option that neither burns the leader's credibility on a suspect nor hands Sam the table: Leo, Lucia, Noah. I have stated plainly that I played Success on Mission 1 — if the table believes the mission evidence, that makes me the cleanest available third alongside two untested players. If this mission fails with me on it, I am a named suspect with nowhere to hide, exactly the accountability standard this table has been demanding all game. Sam's slate asks you to trust a claim; mine asks you to trust a mission result and a risk I am willing to take myself. Lucia, you yielded to me and I owe you a direct answer, so here is my direct question back: if this proposal falls, would you support Leo, Lucia, and Noah as the Mission 2 team — a slate with no member of the failed pair except a leader who has publicly claimed his own Success card, and no seat reserved for the player

Sam here. Two things, quickly.

First, Leo's response was the best counter-argument anyone has made against me, and it still fails. Leo asserts he played a Success card on Mission 1. Nobody can verify that. Mission 1 failed on exactly one Fail card, and Leo is one of the two players I have named as Evil, so his report about his own card is precisely the report with the most motive to be false. Note the asymmetry: Priya has never denied playing that Fail card. If Leo truly played Success, Priya played Fail and she has said nothing. If Leo played Fail, then Priya — who is right now proposing a team that includes herself — has a Fail card available to Mission 2 and has said nothing to disown it. Either way Leo's claim changes nothing about the decision in front of us. It is a self-report by a player with a stake in the outcome, offered to protect a slate that still contains him.

Second, and this part does not depend on whether you take my claim on faith. Priya's proposed team contains Priya. 1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
